lessonTitle: Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis and Gout: Pattern, Pathology, Crystals and Drugs

blocks.text: A 54-year-old man wakes at 3 a.m. after a weekend of beer and shellfish with a hot, red, swollen and exquisitely painful big toe; even the weight of the bedsheet is unbearable. Aspiration of the joint would reveal glittering, needle-shaped crystals engulfed by neutrophils. The pain is not infection and not wear: it is a crystal-driven inflammation, one of three very different reasons a joint can hurt.

blocks.markdown: A synovial joint is lined by articular cartilage over subchondral bone, enclosed by a capsule whose inner **synovium** secretes lubricating fluid. Arthritis can arise from failure of the cartilage (degeneration), autoimmune attack on the synovium, or deposition of crystals that provoke inflammation. The pattern of joints involved and the character of the stiffness give the diagnosis before any test.

### Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis

**Osteoarthritis (OA)** is the commonest joint disease, a degenerative disorder in which articular cartilage is progressively lost under mechanical stress, ageing, obesity or previous injury. Chondrocytes are overwhelmed by matrix-degrading enzymes. The bone beneath responds with **subchondral sclerosis**, **subchondral cysts** and marginal **osteophytes** (bony spurs). It affects weight-bearing and heavily used joints asymmetrically: the knees, hips, spine, the first carpometacarpal joint, and the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (Heberden and Bouchard nodes). Pain is mechanical (worse with use, better with rest) with brief morning stiffness (under about 30 minutes) and no systemic upset.

**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)** is a systemic autoimmune disease in which T cells, B cells and cytokines (tumour necrosis factor alpha, interleukin-6) drive a chronic synovitis. The synovium becomes thickened into a destructive **pannus** that erodes cartilage and bone. It involves the small joints of the hands and feet symmetrically, the **metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and the wrists**, and characteristically **spares the distal interphalangeal joints**. Morning stiffness lasts more than an hour. It has systemic features (fatigue, nodules, anaemia, lung and eye disease), with **rheumatoid factor** and, more specifically, **anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies**, and erosions on radiographs.

blocks.title: Pattern recognition in a painful hand
blocks.prompt: A 62-year-old woman has bony swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints and first carpometacarpal joint, pain after gardening, 15 minutes of morning stiffness, and a normal CRP. A 47-year-old woman has symmetrical swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists, 90 minutes of stiffness and a raised CRP. Which disease does each have?

steps.text: The first woman has DIP and first CMC involvement with use-related pain, brief stiffness and no inflammatory marker rise: this is osteoarthritis (Heberden nodes).
The second has symmetrical MCP and wrist involvement, prolonged morning stiffness and a raised CRP: an inflammatory polyarthritis consistent with rheumatoid arthritis.
Anti-CCP antibodies and radiographic erosions would confirm RA in the second patient.

blocks.answer: First woman: osteoarthritis. Second woman: rheumatoid arthritis.

blocks.markdown:
### Gout and pseudogout

**Gout** is caused by deposition of **monosodium urate (MSU)** crystals in joints in the setting of **hyperuricaemia**, from reduced renal urate excretion or increased production (purine-rich diet, alcohol, diuretics, cell turnover). Urate crystals are phagocytosed by neutrophils and trigger the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1 release, producing sudden severe monoarthritis, classically at the **first metatarsophalangeal joint** (podagra). Chronic deposition forms **tophi**. **Pseudogout** (acute calcium pyrophosphate arthritis) is caused by **calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD)** crystals, usually in older adults, typically in the knee or wrist, and cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) may be seen on radiographs.

blocks.title: Converting urate and judging a target
blocks.prompt: A patient has a serum urate of 9.0 mg/dL. Convert to micromol/L, and compare with a commonly used treatment target of below 360 micromol/L.

steps.text: The target is 360, so the value is well above it. The required fall is 535 - 360 = 175 micromol/L, about 33%.
Long-term urate-lowering therapy is aimed at reaching the target to dissolve crystals and prevent attacks.

blocks.answer: About 535 micromol/L, which exceeds the target of 360 micromol/L.

points: Osteoarthritis is asymmetrical, mechanical, weight-bearing joint degeneration with osteophytes and brief stiffness; rheumatoid arthritis is symmetrical autoimmune synovitis with pannus, long morning stiffness, anti-CCP and sparing of the DIP joints.
Gout shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and pseudogout shows rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals.
Drug classes include NSAIDs, colchicine, corticosteroids, xanthine oxidase inhibitors, conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate, and biologics against TNF, CD20 and the IL-6 receptor.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old retired builder has pain in both knees that worsens after walking and eases with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes and CRP is normal. Radiographs would most likely show which combination?

options.text: Joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis

questions.correctOptionText: Joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these are the radiographic features of osteoarthritis.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: marginal erosions with osteopenia suggest rheumatoid arthritis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: chondrocalcinosis suggests pseudogout and punched-out erosions suggest gout.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: pannus and symmetrical wrist erosions are rheumatoid features.

questions.explanation: Mechanical pain and brief stiffness with normal inflammatory markers indicate osteoarthritis. Cartilage loss narrows the space, while the bone responds with sclerosis and osteophytes.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has symmetrical swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists, morning stiffness of 90 minutes and a raised CRP. Which feature of the history or investigation most favours rheumatoid arthritis over osteoarthritis?

options.text: Positive anti-CCP antibodies with sparing of the distal interphalangeal joints
Heberden nodes at the distal interphalangeal joints

questions.correctOptionText: Positive anti-CCP antibodies with sparing of the distal interphalangeal joints

distractorRationale.a: Correct: anti-CCP is highly specific for RA, and sparing of the DIP joints is typical.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: pain worsened by use is mechanical and suggests osteoarthritis.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: normal inflammatory markers would argue against RA.

questions.explanation: RA is an autoimmune synovitis with symmetrical small joint involvement, and anti-CCP antibodies are specific for it. Distal interphalangeal joint involvement and Heberden nodes would instead point to osteoarthritis.

questions.stem: Joint fluid from an acutely inflamed first metatarsophalangeal joint shows needle-shaped crystals that are strongly negatively birefringent under polarised light. What are they?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gout crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: cholesterol crystals are notched plates and are not typical in acute arthritis.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: calcium oxalate is a renal crystal.

questions.explanation: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals are monosodium urate, which cause gout. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is the classic site.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman presents with an acutely hot, swollen knee after hospital admission for pneumonia. Aspirate shows 20,000 white cells per microlitre, rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals and a negative culture. What is the diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals identify calcium pyrophosphate disease.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: gout has needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: culture is negative and crystals are present, although infection must always be excluded.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: RA does not produce crystals and usually is chronic and symmetrical.

questions.explanation: The crystal shape and weak positive birefringence identify CPPD. Crystal disease is a trigger for acute arthritis in older people, particularly after acute illness, and the knee is a typical site.

questions.stem: Which pairing of drug and mechanism is correct?

options.text: Allopurinol: inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing urate production
Methotrexate: neutralises tumour necrosis factor alpha

questions.correctOptionText: Allopurinol: inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing urate production

distractorRationale.a: Correct: allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: colchicine acts on neutrophil microtubules and not on urate synthesis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: methotrexate is a conventional DMARD, while anti-TNF antibodies neutralise TNF.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: infliximab is an anti-TNF antibody; cyclooxygenase is inhibited by NSAIDs.

questions.explanation: Allopurinol lowers serum urate by inhibiting xanthine oxidase and is used for long-term gout control. The other pairings mismatch the drug and mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient with gout has a serum urate of 7.5 mg/dL. Using the conversion 1 mg/dL = 59.5 micromol/L, calculate the value in micromol/L.
questions.explanation: 7.5 x 59.5 = 446 micromol/L. This exceeds the commonly used treatment target of 360 micromol/L, so urate-lowering therapy would be aimed at reducing it.

questions.stem: A patient on allopurinol has a serum urate of 540 micromol/L and a treatment target of 360 micromol/L. By what percentage must the urate fall to reach the target?
questions.explanation: The required fall is 540 - 360 = 180 micromol/L, and 180 / 540 = 0.333, or 33.3%. Reaching the target keeps serum urate below saturation, so crystals dissolve over time.

questions.stem: Contrast osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis in terms of pattern of joint involvement, pathology and the character of morning stiffness.
markingGuide: OA: asymmetric, weight-bearing joints and DIP, PIP and first CMC joints
RA: symmetric small joints, MCP, PIP, wrists and feet, sparing DIP
OA pathology: cartilage loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
RA pathology: autoimmune synovitis, pannus, cartilage and bone erosion
Stiffness: OA under about 30 minutes; RA over an hour
Systemic features and anti-CCP or rheumatoid factor in RA only
questions.explanation: The distribution and stiffness reflect the different mechanisms, mechanical in OA and inflammatory in RA. The pathology explains the radiographs and the response to disease-modifying treatment.

questions.stem: Describe how gout and pseudogout are distinguished on joint fluid examination, and explain the pathogenesis of an acute gout attack.
markingGuide: Gout: monosodium urate, needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent
Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate, rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent
Both give cloudy fluid with many neutrophils; culture needed to exclude infection
Hyperuricaemia from reduced excretion or increased production leads to crystal deposition
Neutrophils phagocytose crystals, NLRP3 inflammasome activation and interleukin-1 release
First metatarsophalangeal joint typical in gout; knee or wrist in pseudogout
questions.explanation: Polarised light microscopy identifies the crystal by shape and birefringence. In gout the crystals are recognised by the innate immune system, triggering rapid neutrophilic inflammation.

questions.stem: Name five classes of drug used in arthritis, give one example of each and state the mechanism. Explain why urate-lowering therapy is not normally started during an acute gout attack and why methotrexate is classed as a disease-modifying rather than anti-inflammatory drug.
markingGuide: Colchicine: inhibits neutrophil microtubules and inflammasome activity
Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol): reduce urate production
DMARDs: conventional (methotrexate) and biologic (anti-TNF such as adalimumab, rituximab, tocilizumab)
Starting urate-lowering therapy during an attack can mobilise crystals and prolong or worsen the flare, so it is started after the attack settles
DMARDs slow progression of joint damage and take weeks to act, unlike NSAIDs that treat symptoms
questions.explanation: Different classes target pain, inflammation, urate production and the autoimmune process itself. DMARDs alter disease course rather than provide immediate symptom relief, and changing urate levels during an attack can destabilise crystals and aggravate it.
